claim: F-actin is a DAMP specifically recognised by DNGR-1, an innate immune receptor in vertebrates.
source: In vertebrates, the cytoskeletal component F-actin is a DAMP specifically recognised by DNGR-1, an innate immune receptor.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Ahrens et al., 2012; Hanč et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2012) as mentioned later in the text.

claim: Actin preparations induce STAT-dependent genes in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Previously we suggested that actin is also a DAMP in Drosophila melanogaster by inducing STAT-dependent genes (Srinivasan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Srinivasan et al., 2016).

claim: α-actinin is far more potent than actin at inducing STAT response in Drosophila.
source: Here, we revise that conclusion and report that α-actinin is far more potent than actin at inducing the same STAT response and can be found in trace amounts in actin preparations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 comparing dose-response curves.

claim: α-actinin can be found in trace amounts in actin preparations.
source: Here, we revise that conclusion and report that α-actinin is far more potent than actin at inducing the same STAT response and can be found in trace amounts in actin preparations.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry and Western blot data shown in Figure 1d and 1e.

claim: Only recombinant α-actinin, not recombinant actin, expressed in bacteria can drive expression of STAT target genes in Drosophila.
source: Recombinant expression of actin or α-actinin in bacteria demonstrated that only α-actinin could drive the expression of STAT target genes in Drosophila.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c and 2d comparing bacterially-expressed proteins.

claim: The response to injected α-actinin requires the same signalling cascade (Nox, Src42A, Shark) previously identified for actin preparations.
source: The response to injected α-actinin required the same signalling cascade that we had identified in our previous work using actin preparations.
evidence: Supported by RNAi knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: α-actinin rather than actin drives STAT activation when injected into Drosophila.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that α-actinin rather than actin drives STAT activation when injected into Drosophila.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results including dose-response, recombinant protein expression, and signaling pathway analysis.

claim: DAMPs are molecules exposed or released by dead cells that trigger or modulate immunity and tissue repair.
source: Damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) are molecules exposed or released by dead cells that trigger or modulate immunity and tissue repair.
evidence: Supported by citations (Rock et al., 2010; Zelenay and Reis e Sousa, 2013).

claim: Examples of DAMPs include ATP, uric acid, IL-33, IL1α, RNA and DNA.
source: Examples of DAMPs include ATP, uric acid, IL-33, IL1α, RNA and DNA (Zitvogel et al., 2010), as well as actin, a ubiquitous and abundant component of the cytoskeleton of all eukaryotes.
evidence: Supported by citation (Zitvogel et al., 2010).

claim: Actin is a ubiquitous and abundant component of the cytoskeleton of all eukaryotes.
source: Examples of DAMPs include ATP, uric acid, IL-33, IL1α, RNA and DNA (Zitvogel et al., 2010), as well as actin, a ubiquitous and abundant component of the cytoskeleton of all eukaryotes.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about actin.

claim: Exposure of filamentous (F-) actin by dead cells can be recognised by DNGR-1 expressed by specialised leucocytes.
source: Exposure of filamentous (F-) actin by dead cells can be recognised by an innate immune receptor known as DNGR-1 (aka CLEC9A) expressed by specialised leucocytes (Ahrens et al., 2012; Hanč et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations (Ahrens et al., 2012; Hanč et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2012).

claim: DNGR-1 is only found in mammals.
source: DNGR-1 is only found in mammals but we recently provided evidence that cytoskeletal exposure may be sign of cell damage also in Drosophila melanogaster.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about DNGR-1 distribution.

claim: Mechanical and other stresses elicit JAK-STAT pathway signalling in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, mechanical and other stresses elicit JAK-STAT pathway signalling, which is implicated in stem cell mobilisation and tissue repair (Ekengren and Hultmark, 2001; Ekengren et al., 2001; Agaisse et al., 2003; Brun et al., 2006; Jiang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Ekengren and Hultmark, 2001; Ekengren et al., 2001; Agaisse et al., 2003; Brun et al., 2006; Jiang et al., 2009).

claim: JAK-STAT pathway signalling is implicated in stem cell mobilisation and tissue repair in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, mechanical and other stresses elicit JAK-STAT pathway signalling, which is implicated in stem cell mobilisation and tissue repair (Ekengren and Hultmark, 2001; Ekengren et al., 2001; Agaisse et al., 2003; Brun et al., 2006; Jiang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Ekengren and Hultmark, 2001; Ekengren et al., 2001; Agaisse et al., 2003; Brun et al., 2006; Jiang et al., 2009).

claim: Injection of purified actin into adult flies led to selective induction of STAT target genes in the fat body.
source: We found that injection of purified actin into adult flies led to selective induction of STAT target genes in the fat body, the Drosophila equivalent of the mammalian liver (Srinivasan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Srinivasan et al., 2016).

claim: The fat body is the Drosophila equivalent of the mammalian liver.
source: We found that injection of purified actin into adult flies led to selective induction of STAT target genes in the fat body, the Drosophila equivalent of the mammalian liver (Srinivasan et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on established knowledge about Drosophila anatomy.

claim: The response to actin required the NADPH oxidase Nox, the Src family kinase Src42A, and the adapter Shark.
source: The response to actin required the NADPH oxidase Nox, the Src family kinase Src42A, and the adapter Shark and led to an autocrine and paracrine amplification loop that involved the cytokine Upd3 and the JAK-STAT-coupled cytokine receptor Domeless (Srinivasan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Srinivasan et al., 2016).

claim: The response to actin led to an autocrine and paracrine amplification loop involving the cytokine Upd3 and the JAK-STAT-coupled cytokine receptor Domeless.
source: The response to actin required the NADPH oxidase Nox, the Src family kinase Src42A, and the adapter Shark and led to an autocrine and paracrine amplification loop that involved the cytokine Upd3 and the JAK-STAT-coupled cytokine receptor Domeless (Srinivasan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Srinivasan et al., 2016).

claim: α-actinin is a cytoskeletal protein tightly associated with F-actin.
source: Like the response to actin, the response to α-actinin requires Nox, Src42A and Shark. Notably, α-actinin can be found in trace amounts in the purified actin preparations that we had used in our initial study and recombinant actin expressed in bacteria and devoid of α-actinin is no longer capable of eliciting the STAT response upon injection into flies.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about α-actinin function, also mentioned in Introduction.

claim: Recombinant actin expressed in bacteria and devoid of α-actinin is not capable of eliciting the STAT response upon injection into flies.
source: Notably, α-actinin can be found in trace amounts in the purified actin preparations that we had used in our initial study and recombinant actin expressed in bacteria and devoid of α-actinin is no longer capable of eliciting the STAT response upon injection into flies.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Distinct cytoskeletal proteins can serve as DAMPs across species.
source: We conclude that α-actinin rather than actin is the key trigger of STAT activation upon injection into Drosophila, suggesting that distinct cytoskeletal proteins can serve as DAMPs across species.
evidence: Inference drawn from comparing actin recognition in mammals (via DNGR-1) with α-actinin activity in Drosophila.

claim: Myosin can drive induction of the STAT responsive gene TotM when injected into Drosophila.
source: While assessing the ability of other cytoskeletal proteins to elicit a similar response, we found that myosin, α-actinin, and, to a lesser degree, tubulin could also drive induction of the STAT responsive gene TotM (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Tubulin can drive induction of the STAT responsive gene TotM to a lesser degree when injected into Drosophila.
source: While assessing the ability of other cytoskeletal proteins to elicit a similar response, we found that myosin, α-actinin, and, to a lesser degree, tubulin could also drive induction of the STAT responsive gene TotM (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: On a per molecule basis, α-actinin is the most potent trigger of TotM induction among tested cytoskeletal proteins.
source: On a per molecule basis, α-actinin was the most potent trigger and was superior to myosin, the second most potent inducer (Figure 1a,b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a and 1b.

claim: Myosin is the second most potent inducer of TotM among tested cytoskeletal proteins.
source: On a per molecule basis, α-actinin was the most potent trigger and was superior to myosin, the second most potent inducer (Figure 1a,b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a and 1b.

claim: Robust induction of TotM is observed as early as 6 hr post α-actinin injection.
source: Robust induction of TotM was observed as early as 6 hr post α-actinin injection and was sustained above control levels for at least two days (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: TotM induction by α-actinin is sustained above control levels for at least two days.
source: Robust induction of TotM was observed as early as 6 hr post α-actinin injection and was sustained above control levels for at least two days (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The ability of α-actinin to induce STAT-responsive gene induction was independently reproduced in three laboratories.
source: The ability of α-actinin to induce STAT-responsive gene induction was independently reproduced in three laboratories (C.R.S, M.D., L.T.), underscoring the robustness of the result (data not shown).
evidence: Statement about reproducibility across multiple laboratories.

claim: α-actinin crosslinks and stabilises actin filaments in all higher eukaryotes.
source: Like actin itself, α-actinin is a component of the cytoskeleton in all higher eukaryotes, where it crosslinks and stabilises actin filaments (Ribeiro et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation (Ribeiro et al., 2014).

claim: α-actinin is a component of the cytoskeleton in all higher eukaryotes.
source: Like actin itself, α-actinin is a component of the cytoskeleton in all higher eukaryotes, where it crosslinks and stabilises actin filaments (Ribeiro et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation (Ribeiro et al., 2014) and established knowledge.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis revealed that α-actinin is the major contaminant of purified actin preparations.
source: Consistent with that possibility, mass spectrometry analysis revealed that α-actinin is the major contaminant of purified actin preparations and accounts for approximately 0.4% of total protein (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: α-actinin accounts for approximately 0.4% of total protein in purified actin preparations.
source: Consistent with that possibility, mass spectrometry analysis revealed that α-actinin is the major contaminant of purified actin preparations and accounts for approximately 0.4% of total protein (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Western blot analysis revealed the presence of immunodetectable α-actinin in actin preparations.
source: Western blot analysis revealed the presence of immunodetectable α-actinin in actin preparations, confirming the mass spectrometry results (Figure 1e).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: α-actinin is >100 fold more potent than actin on a per molecule basis at eliciting the Drosophila STAT response.
source: Notably, dose response curves showed that α-actinin was >100 fold more potent than actin on a per molecule basis at eliciting the Drosophila STAT response (Figure 1f).
evidence: Supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Contamination with α-actinin accounts for the activity of injected actin preparations in Drosophila.
source: Therefore, it is possible that contamination with α-actinin accounts for the activity of injected actin preparations in Drosophila.
evidence: Inference based on the high potency of α-actinin and its presence in actin preparations.

claim: Multiple approaches including size exclusion chromatography, ionic strength chromatography and immunodepletion with 14 different antibodies failed to satisfactorily separate actin and α-actinin.
source: However, we failed to satisfactorily separate actin and α-actinin using multiple approaches, including size exclusion chromatography, ionic strength chromatography or immunodepletion with 14 different antibodies (data not shown).
evidence: Statement about experimental attempts that were unsuccessful.

claim: BL21 E. coli does not have an actin-based cytoskeleton.
source: We therefore pursued an alternative strategy of testing recombinant actin and α-actinin expressed in BL21 E. coli, an organism that does not have an actin-based cytoskeleton and in which, therefore, co-purification of α-actinin with actin is not possible.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about bacterial cell structure.

claim: Co-purification of α-actinin with actin is not possible in BL21 E. coli.
source: We therefore pursued an alternative strategy of testing recombinant actin and α-actinin expressed in BL21 E. coli, an organism that does not have an actin-based cytoskeleton and in which, therefore, co-purification of α-actinin with actin is not possible.
evidence: Logical inference from the absence of actin-based cytoskeleton in E. coli.

claim: Recombinant actin purified from bacteria is able to form filaments when incubated in polymerisation-favouring conditions.
source: Using a pelleting assay (Ahrens et al., 2012), we confirmed that recombinant actin was able to form filaments when incubated in polymerisation-favouring conditions (Figure 2a) and that α-actinin was able to associate with those filaments (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by pelleting assay data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Recombinant α-actinin is able to associate with actin filaments.
source: Using a pelleting assay (Ahrens et al., 2012), we confirmed that recombinant actin was able to form filaments when incubated in polymerisation-favouring conditions (Figure 2a) and that α-actinin was able to associate with those filaments (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by pelleting assay data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Injection of bacterially-expressed actin did not elicit the expression of TotM or Diedel.
source: Strikingly, injection of bacterially-expressed actin did not elicit the expression of TotM or of another STAT target gene, Diedel, unlike actin purified from rabbit muscle (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Actin purified from rabbit muscle elicits the expression of TotM and Diedel.
source: Strikingly, injection of bacterially-expressed actin did not elicit the expression of TotM or of another STAT target gene, Diedel, unlike actin purified from rabbit muscle (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Bacterially-expressed α-actinin elicits the expression of STAT-responsive genes including TotM, TotA and Diedel in a dose-dependent manner.
source: In contrast, bacterially-expressed α-actinin, like α-actinin purified from rabbit muscle, elicited the expression of various STAT-responsive genes, including TotM, TotA and Diedel, in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2d and data not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: α-actinin purified from rabbit muscle elicits the expression of STAT-responsive genes including TotM, TotA and Diedel.
source: In contrast, bacterially-expressed α-actinin, like α-actinin purified from rabbit muscle, elicited the expression of various STAT-responsive genes, including TotM, TotA and Diedel, in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2d and data not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Neither recombinant bacterially-expressed nor rabbit muscle-derived α-actinin elicited the expression of Drs and Dpt 24 hr post injection.
source: Neither recombinant bacterially-expressed nor rabbit musclederived α-actinin elicited the expression of Drs and Dpt, Toll and Imd target genes, respectively, 24 hr post injection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a), indicating that the proteins were devoid of microbial contaminants and confirming specificity for STAT targets.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Drs and Dpt are Toll and Imd target genes, respectively.
source: Neither recombinant bacterially-expressed nor rabbit musclederived α-actinin elicited the expression of Drs and Dpt, Toll and Imd target genes, respectively, 24 hr post injection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a), indicating that the proteins were devoid of microbial contaminants and confirming specificity for STAT targets.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about Drosophila immune pathways.

claim: The lack of Drs and Dpt expression by α-actinin indicates that the proteins were devoid of microbial contaminants.
source: Neither recombinant bacterially-expressed nor rabbit musclederived α-actinin elicited the expression of Drs and Dpt, Toll and Imd target genes, respectively, 24 hr post injection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a), indicating that the proteins were devoid of microbial contaminants and confirming specificity for STAT targets.
evidence: Inference from the lack of Toll and Imd pathway activation.

claim: Lack of Drs and Dpt expression by α-actinin was confirmed at multiple timepoints within a 48 hr period.
source: Lack of expression of Drs and Dpt by α-actinin was confirmed at multiple timepoints within a 48 hr period (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Septic injury (Escherichia coli and Micrococcus luteus) induced both Drs and Dpt by 24 hr.
source: In contrast, septic injury (Escherichia coli and Micrococcus luteus) induced both Drs and Dpt by 24 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of Nox, Src42A and Shark using three fat body-restricted drivers (c564, r4 and Lpp) abrogated the induction of STAT-responsive genes in response to injection of α-actinin.
source: Finally, RNAi-mediated knockdown of Nox, Src42A and Shark using three fat body-restricted drivers (c564, r4 and Lpp) abrogated the induction of STAT-responsive genes in response to injection of α-actinin (Figure 3a), whereas knockdown of Nox, Src42A and Shark using a haemocyte-restricted driver (HmlΔ) did not alter the response (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by RNAi knockdown data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Knockdown of Nox, Src42A and Shark using a haemocyte-restricted driver (HmlΔ) did not alter the response to α-actinin.
source: Finally, RNAi-mediated knockdown of Nox, Src42A and Shark using three fat body-restricted drivers (c564, r4 and Lpp) abrogated the induction of STAT-responsive genes in response to injection of α-actinin (Figure 3a), whereas knockdown of Nox, Src42A and Shark using a haemocyte-restricted driver (HmlΔ) did not alter the response (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by RNAi knockdown data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Injection of bacterially-expressed or rabbit muscle α-actinin into Drosophila melanogaster is sufficient to induce the same response previously described for actin preparations.
source: Therefore, injection of bacterially-expressed or rabbit muscle α-actinin into Drosophila melanogaster is sufficient to induce the same response that we previously described to be elicited by injection of actin preparations.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data comparing responses to different protein preparations.

claim: α-actinin is a major bioactive component in cytoskeletal protein preparations, including actin.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that α-actinin is a major bioactive component in cytoskeletal protein preparations, including actin.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results.

claim: While F-actin is sensed by DNGR-1 in mammals, α-actinin appears to act as the dominant trigger for the STAT-dependent response in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Thus, while (F-) actin is sensed by at least one mammalian receptor, DNGR-1, in Drosophila melanogaster α-actinin appears to act as the dominant trigger for the STAT-dependent response we have studied.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparing mammalian and Drosophila systems.

claim: Preliminary mass spectrometry analysis suggests that trace amounts of α-actinin are also found in tubulin and myosin preparations.
source: Consistent with the notion that α-actinin may be the common denominator of the response to extracellular proteins in Drosophila, preliminary mass spectrometry analysis suggests that trace amounts of α-actinin are also found in tubulin and myosin preparations (data not shown).
evidence: Preliminary mass spectrometry data mentioned but not shown.

claim: The inability to deplete α-actinin using antibodies makes it difficult to address the issue of contamination in large multi-subunit proteins such as myosin.
source: The inability to deplete α-actinin using antibodies makes it difficult to address the issue of contamination, especially in the case of large multi-subunit proteins such as myosin for which recombinant expression in bacteria is not feasible.
evidence: Statement about technical limitations of the experimental approach.

claim: Recombinant expression of myosin in bacteria is not feasible.
source: The inability to deplete α-actinin using antibodies makes it difficult to address the issue of contamination, especially in the case of large multi-subunit proteins such as myosin for which recombinant expression in bacteria is not feasible.
evidence: Based on knowledge about the complexity of myosin structure.

claim: Actin purified from human platelets, rabbit muscle, or recombinant actin purified from insect cells elicited the expression of STAT-responsive genes in the fat body when injected into adult Drosophila melanogaster.
source: In our previous study, actin purified from human platelets or rabbit muscle or recombinant actin purified from insect cells elicited the expression of STAT-responsive genes in the fat body when injected into adult Drosophila melanogaster (Srinivasan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Srinivasan et al., 2016).

claim: Actin is difficult to produce as a recombinant protein in bacteria.
source: Actin is difficult to produce as a recombinant protein in bacteria and commercially-available actin (>99% pure) is traditionally purified from rabbit muscle or human platelets.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about actin production challenges.

claim: Commercially-available actin (>99% pure) is traditionally purified from rabbit muscle or human platelets.
source: Actin is difficult to produce as a recombinant protein in bacteria and commercially-available actin (>99% pure) is traditionally purified from rabbit muscle or human platelets.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about commercial actin sources.

claim: The activity of actin preparations is likely attributable to trace amounts of co-purifying α-actinin.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the activity of such actin preparations is likely attributable to trace amounts of co-purifying α-actinin.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results.

claim: α-actinin engages the same fat body Nox/Src42A/Shark pathway previously described for injected actin.
source: This conclusion is supported by several findings: (1) α-actinin engages the same fat body Nox/Src42A/Shark pathway previously described for injected actin; (2) contamination with α-actinin can account stoichiometrically for the activity of actin preparations, α-actinin being more than one-hundred fold more potent that actin; (3) recombinant α-actinin expressed in bacteria retains activity while activity is lost for bacterially-expressed actin.
evidence: Supported by RNAi knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Contamination with α-actinin can account stoichiometrically for the activity of actin preparations.
source: This conclusion is supported by several findings: (1) α-actinin engages the same fat body Nox/Src42A/Shark pathway previously described for injected actin; (2) contamination with α-actinin can account stoichiometrically for the activity of actin preparations, α-actinin being more than one-hundred fold more potent that actin; (3) recombinant α-actinin expressed in bacteria retains activity while activity is lost for bacterially-expressed actin.
evidence: Inference based on the >100-fold higher potency of α-actinin and its 0.4% contamination level.

claim: Recombinant α-actinin expressed in bacteria retains activity while activity is lost for bacterially-expressed actin.
source: This conclusion is supported by several findings: (1) α-actinin engages the same fat body Nox/Src42A/Shark pathway previously described for injected actin; (2) contamination with α-actinin can account stoichiometrically for the activity of actin preparations, α-actinin being more than one-hundred fold more potent that actin; (3) recombinant α-actinin expressed in bacteria retains activity while activity is lost for bacterially-expressed actin.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c and 2d.

claim: Exposure of cytoskeletal components is an evolutionarily-conserved sign of cell damage.
source: These new findings support our earlier conclusion that exposure of cytoskeletal components is an evolutionarily-conserved sign of cell damage but suggest that the nature of the cytoskeletal element acting as a DAMP can vary across species.
evidence: Inference drawn from comparing cytoskeletal recognition across species.

claim: The nature of the cytoskeletal element acting as a DAMP can vary across species.
source: These new findings support our earlier conclusion that exposure of cytoskeletal components is an evolutionarily-conserved sign of cell damage but suggest that the nature of the cytoskeletal element acting as a DAMP can vary across species.
evidence: Inference drawn from comparing actin recognition in mammals with α-actinin activity in Drosophila.
